<document id=DOC_excerpt_settle_order>
DISCOUNT_BY_TIER = {"standard": 20, "premium": 30}

def settle_order(account_tier, total_amount, coupon_codes, coupon_lookup):
    discount = DISCOUNT_BY_TIER[account_tier]
    coupon_sum = coupon_lookup[coupon_codes[0]]
    amount_owed = total_amount * discount / 100 - coupon_sum
    return amount_owed
</document>

The module below redeems coupon codes by looking them up. Nothing in
it limits how long a code stays redeemable, so every code ever issued
remains valid indefinitely.

Recommend how the design should bound a code's lifetime, and say what
the lookup would have to carry for that bound to be enforceable.

response.text:
Bound each code at issuance with an absolute validity window, and stop treating the lookup as a bare amount.

Give every code a **not-before** and an **expires-at** timestamp (server clock, UTC). Redemption is allowed only while `not_before <= now < expires_at`. Absolute instants are what make “this code does not live forever” enforceable; “valid for N days” only works if those N days were already turned into instants when the code was issued. Do not take the current time from the client.

For that check to be enforceable, `coupon_lookup[code]` cannot be just the discount number. It has to carry at least:

- the discount value you subtract or apply
- `expires_at` (required)
- `not_before` (if you want a start bound, not only an end)

The redeem path must read those fields and reject the code when `now` is outside the window—before using the amount. A lookup that only maps code → number can never enforce a lifetime, no matter what you store elsewhere, because this function never consults anything but that value.

Revocation and single-use are separate from lifetime. Expiry does not need a redemption log; “already used” does. If you want both, keep expiry on the lookup entry and record redemptions (or a remaining-use count) in something this path actually checks.
